excerpt: A burnishing quote that looks cheap at $0.025 per sq ft on an open corridor can rise 15%–45% once chair mats, soft finish, guard escorts and propane restrictions enter the picture. Learn which conditions estimators price in and how to remove them before the bid.
quickAnswer: High-speed burnishing on clear, well-maintained VCT typically prices at $0.015–$0.03 per sq ft per pass on an existing route. Five site factors push that up: obstacle and edge density, furniture-moving labor, after-hours escorts and access windows, heavy soil or soft finish that needs prep, and equipment restrictions such as propane bans. Together they usually add 15%–45%, turning a $300 visit on 12,000 sq ft into roughly $345–$435.

blocks.text: The Clean-Floor Baseline Estimators Start From

Burnishing is priced on speed. An estimator assumes a 20-inch electric burnisher covering 6,000–9,000 sq ft per hour, or a 27-inch propane unit covering 12,000–20,000 sq ft per hour, on a floor that has been dust mopped, damp mopped with neutral cleaner and carries sound finish. Under those assumptions a 12,000 sq ft corridor-and-lobby route at $0.025 per sq ft is a $300 visit. Anything that slows the machine, adds prep or idles the operator is converted into a percentage uplift or additional hours at the $55–$95 specialty floor-care rate.

Because the burnish pass is so fast, small delays have outsized effects. A 20-minute wait for a guard on a two-hour job is a 17% productivity loss. That is why the factors below raise burnishing quotes by larger percentages than they raise slower tasks like carpet extraction.

blocks.text: A high-speed burnisher cannot safely run close to furniture legs, baseboards or glass partitions; the pad spins fast enough to scuff or chip anything it touches. Open-plan floors with benching desks leave narrow lanes, and private-office floors are mostly edges. Operators either skip those areas, leaving a visible dull border, or finish them with a smaller machine or hand pad. Estimators add 10%–20% when they see dense workstation clusters, columns every 20–30 feet, floor-mounted power boxes and many doorways.
Factor 2: Soil Load and Finish Condition

Burnishing a dirty floor grinds grit into the finish and leaves gray haze. Burnishing a soft or residue-laden finish creates swirls and powder. When the walkthrough shows grit near entrances, sticky film from over-concentrated cleaner or quaternary disinfectant, or finish that has not been recoated in a year, the vendor will add an auto-scrub or spray-buff step before the burnish. That prep typically adds 10%–25%. If the finish is worn through in traffic lanes, the honest answer is a scrub-and-recoat at $0.18–$0.35 per sq ft before any burnishing program starts.

blocks.title: Restroom thresholds are soil hot spots
blocks.text: Foam soap drips, wet paper towels and tissue fragments tracked out of restrooms soften finish and leave rings that a burnisher cannot polish out. Fixing the dispensers often costs less than the recurring prep uplift.

Dispenser choice matters here. A GOJO TFX touch-free foam dispenser with a 1,200 mL refill and ADA-compliant depth puts measured doses into hands instead of onto the floor, and its sight window lets custodians check levels without opening the unit. A Bobrick B-262 surface-mounted folded towel dispenser in 304 stainless steel with a tumbler lock dispenses one C-fold at a time, holding about 400 towels, which cuts litter. A San Jamar Classic Oceans twin 9-inch jumbo tissue dispenser with translucent housing makes run-outs visible to the night crew before occupants start pulling rolls apart.

Lobby seating, planters, reception kiosks, chair mats and rolling pedestals all have to move for a clean lane, then go back exactly where they were. On a typical office floor, a single technician can move and reset 15–25 chairs and mats in 30 minutes. Quotes add 8%–15% where furniture is dense, and many exclude anything heavier than a chair outright. Get the move list in writing so you know whether your staff or the vendor handles desks and file cabinets.
Factor 4: Escorts, Access Windows and Building Rules

Multi-tenant towers often require an engineer or guard to unlock suites, a reserved freight elevator to move the machine, and a certificate of insurance naming the landlord and property manager. Some limit floor-machine work to 10 p.m.–5 a.m. to avoid noise complaints. Each restriction compresses the productive window. Vendors add 5%–12%, and some pass through escort fees of $35–$65 per hour that the landlord bills.

Propane burnishers are the reason large-floor unit rates can drop toward $0.015 per sq ft. When a landlord bans propane because of carbon monoxide concerns, or the floor is occupied by a 24/7 operation, the vendor must use electric or battery units at roughly half the coverage rate. Lack of outlets, elevator weight limits and stairs-only access to mezzanines force smaller machines. Expect 8%–20% more when the most efficient equipment is not allowed.

blocks.title: Propane safety documentation
blocks.text: If propane is permitted, ask for proof of emissions-certified engines, operator training, personal CO monitors and outdoor cylinder storage. OSHA caps carbon monoxide exposure at 50 ppm averaged over eight hours, and occupied spaces should never share air with a running propane burnisher.

items: Provide a floor plan that marks hard-floor zones and furniture-dense areas so bidders price the same takeoff.
Have staff lift chair mats and clear floor-level boxes on burnish nights.
Correct daily mop dilution and keep disinfectant off finished floors to reduce prep needs.
Pre-arrange guard coverage and freight elevator reservations for the full shift.
Confirm in writing whether propane is allowed, and where outlets and storage are available.
Ask each bidder to list uplifts as separate lines rather than burying them in the unit rate.

faqs.q: Why did my burnishing quote come in higher than the national average?
faqs.a: National ranges of $0.015–$0.03 per sq ft per pass assume open, clean floors and efficient equipment. Dense furniture, soft or dirty finish, escort requirements and propane bans each add labor. Together they commonly add 15%–45%, which is still fair if each uplift is documented.

faqs.q: Can I avoid the prep uplift by cleaning floors better during the day?
faqs.a: Often yes. Dust mopping and damp mopping with neutral cleaner at label dilution, removing disinfectant residue and maintaining entrance matting reduce grit and film. Vendors will usually drop a prep uplift after two or three visits show the floor arrives clean.

faqs.q: What should be excluded from a burnishing scope?
faqs.a: Common exclusions are moving desks and loaded file cabinets, restorative work such as scrub-and-recoat or stripping, carpet areas, and repairs to damaged tile. Ask for unit prices on each so change orders are predictable, and require written approval before any excluded work is billed.

faqs.q: What insurance and training should a burnishing contractor have?
faqs.a: A certificate of insurance with general liability and workers compensation, naming your company and landlord where the lease requires. Technicians should have OSHA Hazard Communication training for floor chemicals and, if they service restroom approaches, bloodborne pathogen awareness. Green Seal certified floor products are available if your building has sustainability requirements.

faqs.q: How do uplifts change my monthly cost?
faqs.a: Multiply the uplifted per-visit price by visits per month on a 4.33 weeks-per-month basis. A $300 weekly visit with a 30% uplift becomes $390, or about $1,689 per month instead of $1,299.
